name: Thermage FLX

lead: Thermage FLX is a clinic-based machine that uses monopolar radiofrequency energy to tighten lax skin and soften wrinkles on the face, eye area, neck and body without surgery. The Thermage line was the first monopolar RF skin-tightening system FDA-cleared, for the eye area in 2002.

RF current is converted to heat by tissue resistance, warming the dermis while surface cooling protects the skin. The heat is said to contract existing collagen right away and trigger new collagen over weeks to months. Research is largely small studies, practitioner surveys and device-company-linked trials, with reports of gradual, modest improvement over months.

paras: Trained clinicians deliver it in a single office session. Results build over several months and are described as lasting about one to two years. In forums it is discussed as a non-surgical option for jawline and facial laxity.

Reported effects include redness, swelling and pain, with burns, blistering, pigment change, dents, scarring and fat loss described less commonly. Pacemakers and pregnancy are listed contraindications.

web.title: Radio-frequency skin tightening (Wikipedia, via Thermage redirect)

angle.text: Thermage FLX is used to tighten the face, eye area and body and soften wrinkles without surgery. Radiofrequency heats the deep skin, contracting collagen and prompting new collagen over months. The evidence is many small studies and few controlled trials.

lead: Thermage FLX is a monopolar radiofrequency (RF) device used in aesthetic medicine to heat the deeper layers of the skin with the aim of tightening lax skin and reducing wrinkles without surgery. It is the latest generation of the Thermage line, which is described as the first monopolar RF skin-tightening system to receive US FDA clearance, for periorbital (eye-area) use in 2002 [1].

Radio-frequency skin tightening in general passes alternating current through tissue, which resists the current and converts it to heat; the dermis is heated while skin cooling protects the surface [2][1]. Proponents and device makers say the heat causes immediate collagen contraction and later new collagen formation, with effects building over several months [2][1]. Treatments are delivered by clinicians in office settings.

Published evidence on Thermage-type monopolar RF consists mainly of small, often single-arm, studies and clinician surveys, such as a questionnaire of 52 Korean dermatologists on the FLX version [3] and a 20-patient single-arm study of RF combined with fractional laser [4]. Grokipedia notes that many studies are small and lack randomized controls [1]. In forum culture, devices of this type are discussed as a non-surgical option for jawline and facial laxity.
infobox: Thermage (now marketed by Solta Medical, per Wikipedia)[2]
Dermis (typically about 3-4 mm depth, per Grokipedia)[1]
Immediate tightening, with gradual change over about 3-6 months (reported)[1]

paras: Wikipedia lists the Thermage system among commercial RF skin-tightening devices and places it in a category that also includes bipolar, tripolar and microneedle RF systems from other manufacturers [2]. In monopolar systems a single treatment electrode delivers energy and a return pad completes the circuit, which is generally described as allowing deeper heating than bipolar designs [2][1].

The Thermage FLX is described as a newer-generation handpiece system used for the face, neck and body [1]. A treatment session is reported to take roughly 30 minutes to 2 hours depending on area, with results developing over months [1].

According to Grokipedia, RF energy entered medicine as electrosurgery in the 1920s and dermatology later used it to destroy lesions; in the 1990s interest shifted to non-ablative heating, and the monopolar Thermage device received FDA clearance for periorbital tightening in 2002, with full-face clearance cited for 2004 [1]. The FLX version is reported to have been cleared in 2017 [1]. A 2011 article on a competing RF device likewise dates the market for non-ablative RF heating devices to the introduction of Thermage in 2002.

RF energy at frequencies of roughly 0.3 to 10 MHz is converted to heat by tissue resistance; heat is aimed at the dermis while the epidermis is protected by cooling [1]. Wikipedia gives an ideal dermal target temperature of 67 degrees C, noting that the claim relates to delivering power until that temperature is reached [2]. Heating is said to cause immediate collagen fibre shrinkage followed by fibroblast activity and neocollagenesis over weeks to months [1]. Histology studies cited by Grokipedia reported increased type I collagen at three months [1].

Early Thermage studies cited by Grokipedia reported that about 83% of 86 periorbital patients improved by at least one grade on a wrinkle scale after one treatment [1]. The same source summarises typical reported outcomes as modest immediate tightening that increases over several months and lasts around one to two years, while noting the evidence base is dominated by small, non-randomized studies [1].

In a survey of 52 Korean dermatologists, the FLX was rated more effective by 57.4% and faster with shorter treatment time by 66.0% than earlier versions, while 25.5% found it more painful [3]. Survey data reflect practitioner opinion rather than controlled outcome measurement.

Wikipedia reports that some patients have experienced pain requiring sedation, that improper application can leave skin dents from uneven healing, and that fat necrosis and atrophic scarring have been reported with RF devices [2]. Grokipedia lists redness, swelling and mild pain lasting one to three days as common, blistering, burns and hyperpigmentation as less common, and pacemakers, defibrillators and pregnancy as contraindications [1].
Pain is described as a barrier to treatment completion. A 2026 prospective study examined whether pain perception during monopolar RF facial therapy differed by side of the face and by age [5].

Published human data include a 52-respondent practitioner survey of the FLX [3] and a prospective single-arm study of 20 women with mild to moderate facial laxity who received monopolar RF combined with fractional diode laser treatments [4]. A 2026 prospective study looked at pain perception during monopolar RF facial therapy [5].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists several registered Thermage FLX studies, including a 164-participant prospective controlled safety and effectiveness study started in 2025 [6], a 25-participant study of face, neck and eyelid treatment started in 2019 [7], and a 12-participant study of the lower face and submentum completed after a 2020 start [8]. Results for these registrations are not summarised here.

timeline.event: Monopolar Thermage receives US FDA clearance for periorbital tightening, according to Grokipedia.[1]
Thermage FLX reported as FDA 510(k) cleared.[1]
A controlled safety and effectiveness study of Thermage FLX (n=164) begins; listed as active, not recruiting.[6]
